RECAP: Session 12 : Cloud Security & Shared Responsibility
1. Security Goals: Confidentiality, integrity & availability in the cloud
2. Shared Responsibility Model: Security of the cloud vs security in the cloud
3. Responsibility by Service Model: Boundary shifts across IaaS, PaaS & SaaS
4. Common Misunderstandings: Provider vs customer duties; incidents caused by wrong assumptions
5. Defense in Depth: Layered controls: network, identity, data, application & monitoring

Agenda for Today's Session
1. Identity in the Cloud: Root & owner account; users; groups
2. Authentication vs Authorization: Identity verification vs permission checking; credentials: passwords, access keys & tokens
3. Policy Structure: Effect, action, resource & condition; identity-based vs resource-based policies
4. Policy Evaluation Logic: Default deny; explicit allow; explicit deny precedence; combining multiple policies
5. Reading a Denial: Access-denied messages; audit logs; tracing a denial to its statement

slides.title: Cloud Identity Types
slides.lead: Every cloud platform uses identities to identify who is making a request and determine what actions they are allowed to perform. Cloud identity is built from three layers: the root account, individual users, and groups

rows: AWS IAM: Identity and Access Management manages identities and controls their permissions
Root or owner account: created automatically when the cloud account signs up
IAM user: a separate identity for one person or application
Group: a named collection of users sharing one set of permissions

slides.notes: Open by framing identity as the first question any permission check asks. Name AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) as the service managing all three layers. Exam angle: distinguishing root account from an IAM user is a frequent interview question.

slides.title: Full Account Owner
slides.lead: The root account is the single identity automatically created when a cloud account is opened; it owns the account and starts with unrestricted access to every resource and the billing page

points.text: Signs in with the email used to create the account, not a username
Needed for special tasks such as account closure, changing root credentials, and enabling IAM user billing access
AWS recommends enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) and avoiding daily use

slides.notes: Stress that root is not meant for daily work; IAM users exist for that. Point out that account closure and enabling IAM access to billing are root-only actions. Exam angle: why locking away root credentials matters is a common interview question.

slides.label: Analogy: company owner's master key
slides.title: Full Account Owner
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A company owner's master key opens every office and controls all important operations, so it is kept secure and used only when necessary: just as the root account has complete control over AWS resources and should not be used for daily tasks.

Stress that root is not meant for daily work; IAM users exist for that. Point out that account closure and enabling IAM access to billing are root-only actions. Exam angle: why locking away root credentials matters is a common interview question.

slides.title: Individual Vs Collective
slides.lead: Below the root account, an IAM user is a separate identity given to one person or application, each with its own credentials and permissions

points.text: Group: a named bucket of users that share one policy set
Adding a user to a group grants every group permission at once
Removing a user from a group revokes those permissions instantly

slides.notes: Explain that groups exist so permissions are managed once, not per user. Point to the group box absorbing three users as one unit. Exam angle: why groups scale better than per-user policies is often asked.

slides.title: Root Users Groups
slides.lead: Cloud teams rarely use the root account after initial setup, relying instead on IAM users and groups managed from the IAM console's Users and Groups pages

cells: Initial setup and a few root-only tasks, such as account closure
Daily work for a person or app
Shared permission set for many users
None directly: a group cannot sign in; members inherit its permissions

note.text: Knowing who is asking is the first half of access control; the next step checks whether that identity is who it claims to be

slides.notes: Point to the IAM console's Users and Groups tabs as the real screens where these identities are managed. Note root account settings sit under the account name dropdown, not IAM. Exam angle: matching each identity type to its correct use case is commonly tested.

slides.title: Two Access Checks
slides.lead: Every cloud request passes through two separate checks before it runs: one confirms who is asking, the other confirms what that identity may do

points.text: Credentials carry the proof: passwords, access keys, tokens
Permission failure returns a different error type than an identity failure
Identity and permission checks are performed when accessing protected cloud resources, not just at sign-in

slides.notes: Set up the two-step gate before naming either check in depth. Mention this split is exactly what an interviewer tests with 'what is the difference between authentication and authorization'.

slides.title: Verifying Identity First
slides.lead: Before any action is allowed, the caller's identity must be confirmed. Authentication is this first check: proving the caller truly is the identity it claims to be

rows: Console sign-in needs a username, password and optional MFA code
Programmatic calls sign each request with an access key pair
Root account authenticates separately from every IAM user
Authentication failure stops the request before authorization runs

slides.notes: Explain that this is the sign-in step, not the permission step. Point out the root account and IAM user both go through this gate separately, which is a common interview trap.

slides.label: Analogy: exam hall
slides.title: Verifying Identity First
slides.notes:
TR analogy: At an exam hall, the invigilator checks the hall ticket and ID card to confirm the student is who they claim to be: just as authentication checks credentials to confirm the caller's identity.

Explain that this is the sign-in step, not the permission step. Point out the root account and IAM user both go through this gate separately, which is a common interview trap.

slides.title: Checking Granted Permission
slides.lead: Confirming identity does not say what that identity may do. Authorization is the check that follows: whether the now-verified identity holds permission for this action on this resource

rows: Authorization runs only after authentication succeeds
Policies attached to an identity define its permissions
One identity can be allowed one action and denied another
A valid login with no matching policy still gets denied

slides.notes: Stress the sequence: identity first, permission second, never the reverse. Flag that an interviewer often asks for a real example, so mention denying delete while allowing read for the same user.

slides.label: Analogy: housing society guard
slides.title: Checking Granted Permission
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A housing society guard who already confirmed a visitor's identity still checks the visitor pass for permitted floors: just as authorization checks a verified identity's permissions before allowing a specific action.

Stress the sequence: identity first, permission second, never the reverse. Flag that an interviewer often asks for a real example, so mention denying delete while allowing read for the same user.

slides.title: Proving Identity
slides.lead: Cloud identities present different proof depending on how they connect: a human at the console, or code calling an application programming interface (API)

cells: Console sign-in by a human user
Long-lived; MFA adds an extra layer
Long-lived until deactivated, deleted, or rotated
Calls made via an assumed role

note.text: Role: an identity with no password or keys of its own; whoever assumes it gets a temporary token

slides.notes: Walk the three rows left to right, naming where each credential is issued. Note that a leaked access key is a common exam and interview question on cloud security.

slides.title: Where They Live
slides.lead: Each credential type is issued and managed from a specific screen inside Identity and Access Management, the console section that administers cloud identities

points.text: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues tokens for an assumed role, valid for 15 minutes to 12 hours
Password policy sets minimum length, rotation and reuse rules
MFA registration links a virtual authenticator, passkey or hardware device to the user
Key rotation needs old key deactivated before deletion, not after

note.text: Every decision made with these credentials is governed by policies

slides.notes: Name the exact IAM console locations rather than describing them generically. This bridges naturally into how a policy document actually decides allow or deny.

slides.label: Quiz Time
slides.notes: Quiz on Identity in the Cloud and Authentication vs Authorization. Q1. Which identity is created automatically when a cloud account is opened? Answer: The root account. Q2. Why should the root account not be used for daily work? Answer: It has unrestricted access to every resource and to billing; AWS recommends MFA and avoiding daily use. Q3. What does adding a user to a group do? Answer: The user gets every permission of that group at once. Q4. Can a group sign in? Answer: No; a group has no credentials, its members inherit its permissions. Q5. Which check runs first, authentication or authorization? Answer: Authentication, which proves who the caller is. Q6. A user signs in successfully but no policy allows the action. What happens? Answer: The request is denied. Q7. Which credential does a CLI or SDK call use? Answer: An access key (ID and secret). Q8. Which AWS service issues temporary tokens for an assumed role? Answer: AWS Security Token Service (STS).

slides.title: Rules As Documents
slides.lead: An IAM policy is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document that states a rule for cloud access requests

points.text: Allow or Deny is the only outcome a statement can declare
The operation controlled is named precisely, such as reading a file
The exact item the operation applies to is always identified
An extra requirement can narrow when the rule applies

slides.notes: Introduce the policy document as the written rule AWS checks before any access request. Point out that IAM policies are built in the IAM console's policy editor. Interviewers often ask to name all four elements — stress that Condition is optional.

slides.title: Rules As Documents

fields: Version: the policy language version, written as 2012-10-17
Statement: holds one or more rules
Sid: an optional name for a statement

slides.notes: Introduce the policy document as the written rule AWS checks before any access request. Point out that IAM policies are built in the IAM console's policy editor. Interviewers often ask to name all four elements — stress that Condition is optional.

slides.label: Analogy: train ticket
slides.title: Rules As Documents
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A train ticket states exactly what is allowed: travel on one train, in one seat, on one date: just as a policy states the effect, the action, the resource and the condition for a request.

Introduce the policy document as the written rule AWS checks before any access request. Point out that IAM policies are built in the IAM console's policy editor. Interviewers often ask to name all four elements — stress that Condition is optional.

slides.title: Outcome And Operation
slides.lead: Effect sets the policy's outcome, while Action names the exact operation being controlled; together they state what is being decided before resource and condition narrow it further
slides.notes: Explain that Action always follows service:operation syntax, using S3 GetObject as the example. Mention the IAM visual editor lets an action be picked from a dropdown instead of typed by hand. Exam tip: a wildcard in Action is a common least-privilege anti-pattern.

slides.title: Outcome And Operation

points.text: Action supports wildcards, e.g. s3:* for all S3 operations
A single statement can list several actions together
Effect allows only two values, never a partial grant

slides.notes: Explain that Action always follows service:operation syntax, using S3 GetObject as the example. Mention the IAM visual editor lets an action be picked from a dropdown instead of typed by hand. Exam tip: a wildcard in Action is a common least-privilege anti-pattern.

slides.title: Target And Constraint
slides.lead: Resource pins the action to a specific item or group of items, identified by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN), while Condition adds an extra test that must also be true before the effect applies

points.text: ARN format: arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource (some fields can be empty, as in S3 ARNs)
An S3 object ARN example is arn:aws:s3:::finance-reports/jan.pdf
Condition keys check IP address, time window or MFA status
Resource can use wildcards to cover a group of items

slides.notes: Walk through the ARN example field by field, pointing at the resource segment. Note the Resource and Condition fields both sit in the IAM policy JSON tab, editable directly. A frequent interview question asks to write an ARN for a specific S3 object.

slides.title: Where It Attaches
slides.lead: Every policy statement is attached somewhere: either to the identity making the request or to the resource receiving it. These are the two most common policy types in AWS

rows: Identity-based: attached to a user, group or role
Resource-based: attached directly to the resource, e.g. a bucket
Identity-based policies are the default for most access setups

slides.notes: Clarify that identity-based policies travel with the user wherever they go, while resource-based policies stay fixed to that one resource. Point to the bucket policy tab inside the S3 console as a resource-based example.

slides.title: Where It Attaches
slides.lead: A resource-based policy names who gets the access in one more element, Principal, which is how one AWS account can grant access to another

rows: A resource-based policy has one more element, Principal, which names who gets the access
Resource-based policies can grant access to another AWS account

slides.notes: Point to Principal as the element only a resource-based policy has: it names who gets the access. Interviewers test whether a bucket policy or an IAM policy is needed for cross-account sharing.

slides.label: Analogy: office access
slides.title: Where It Attaches
slides.notes:
TR analogy: An office employee can carry an access card with assigned permissions, or a restricted room can have an approved visitor list: just as an identity-based policy is attached to a user, while a resource-based policy is attached to the resource.

Clarify that identity-based policies travel with the user wherever they go, while resource-based policies stay fixed to that one resource. Point to the bucket policy tab inside the S3 console as a resource-based example. Interviewers test whether a bucket policy or an IAM policy is needed for cross-account sharing.

slides.title: Side By Side
slides.lead: Choosing between the two types depends on who owns the access decision: the identity side or the resource side

head: Aspect
Identity-Based
Resource-Based
rows: The resource itself, e.g. a bucket
Supported natively; the other account must also allow it
props.note: AWS evaluates applicable policies together to determine whether a request is allowed or denied

slides.notes: Use this table to contrast where each policy type lives and how cross-account access differs. Point to the IAM policy list versus an S3 bucket's permissions tab. Mention that the deny-by-default evaluation logic applies identically to both types, which comes next.

slides.title: Four Decision Steps
slides.lead: Without a fixed decision path, two conflicting permissions could leave a request's outcome unpredictable; cloud providers resolve this with one strict evaluation order

points.text: Combining policies: all attached policies are merged before deciding
Default deny: no access unless a rule allows it
Explicit deny: any deny statement overrides every allow
Explicit allow: a statement must grant the action

note.text: The IAM Policy Simulator helps test how IAM policies affect access decisions without making actual AWS requests

slides.notes: Walk the flowchart top to bottom before naming each step on its own. Point to the deny branch as the override to remember. Exam angle: evaluation order is a frequent interview question.

slides.title: Nothing Allowed First
slides.lead: Before any rule is checked, identity and access management starts from a closed position: a request is rejected unless a policy explicitly permits it

points.text: Default deny: the starting state for every request, except those made by the root user
Explicit allow: only an Effect Allow statement passes it
Silence is denial: an unmentioned action is never granted by omission

note.text: This default state is visible in the AWS IAM console, where a new user with no attached policy cannot perform any action

slides.notes: Stress that silence means denial, a common exam trap. Explain in plain words: no rule equals no entry. Ask why default deny is safer than default allow.

slides.label: Analogy: phone app permissions
slides.title: Nothing Allowed First
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A new phone app cannot touch the camera or contacts until the user grants each permission: exactly as IAM blocks every request until an explicit allow statement is matched.

Stress that silence means denial, a common exam trap. Explain in plain words: no rule equals no entry. Ask why default deny is safer than default allow.

slides.title: Precedence Rule
slides.lead: An explicit deny in any applicable policy beats every allow, even one written with broader scope, so a safety rule can never be bypassed by accident

points.text: Evaluation checks for an explicit deny across all matched policies first
One deny statement blocks the action regardless of how many allows exist
An allow from any other policy cannot cancel a matching deny
Used to lock sensitive actions irrespective of other granted permissions

slides.notes: State the one-line rule: deny beats allow, no matter the source. Point to the two boxes collapsing into one denied outcome. Exam angle: this precedence is tested with multi-policy scenarios.

slides.title: Identity Plus Resource
slides.lead: Access decisions often combine an identity-based policy attached to a user with a resource-based policy attached to the resource, such as a storage bucket

cells: Deny s3:GetObject when the source IP is outside 203.0.113.0/24

slides.notes: Trace the IP check live: allowed by A, trapped by B's condition. Point to the condition clause as the exact cause of denial. Exam angle: combining identity and resource policies is common in cross-account questions.

slides.title: Identity Plus Resource
slides.lead: A request from IP 198.51.100.7 is evaluated: Policy A allows it, but the IP is outside Policy B's range, so the deny applies and the request is rejected
slides.notes: Trace the IP check live: allowed by A, trapped by B's condition. Point to the condition clause as the exact cause of denial. Exam angle: combining identity and resource policies is common in cross-account questions.

slides.title: Union With Deny Override
slides.lead: All identity-based and resource-based policies that apply to a request are evaluated together: allows add up, and an explicit deny overrides them

points.text: Allow permissions from several identity-based policies on one user add together
Cross-account sharing needs agreement from both the identity side and the resource side
Within one account, an allow in either the identity-based or the resource-based policy is enough

slides.notes: Summarise the merge rule in one line: allows add up, one deny removes. Point to the IAM Policy Simulator as where this logic is checked in the console. The next section traces this logic through a real denial message.

slides.title: Three Pieces of Evidence
slides.lead: A denied request is not a dead end: it leaves three pieces of evidence that together explain why it failed

points.text: The denial message: who tried what, on which resource
The audit log: a timestamped record of the call itself
The policy statement: the exact rule that produced the deny, or the missing allow

slides.notes: Frame this as detective work: each box narrows down the cause. Mention this reasoning is used constantly when debugging IAM in interviews.

slides.title: What AWS Reports
slides.lead: Cloud providers return a structured error when a request is refused, naming the identity, the action and the resource involved: not just the word denied

points.text: The denial message may identify the user or role that made the call
The specific operation attempted is reported, such as deleting an object
The exact target object or service is identified in the message
A reason hint distinguishes an explicit deny from no matching allow

props.sample: User: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/alice is not authorized to perform: s3:DeleteObject on resource: arn:aws:s3:::finance-reports/q1.csv with an explicit deny in an identity-based policy

slides.notes: Read a sample denial message aloud and point to each underlined part. Ask: which part tells us WHY, versus just WHAT failed?

slides.label: Analogy: failed UPI payment
slides.title: What AWS Reports
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A failed UPI payment shows who paid, how much, to whom and the reason, such as insufficient balance: just as an AWS denial message shows who made the request, the action, the resource and why it was denied.

Read a sample denial message aloud and point to each underlined part. Ask: which part tells us WHY, versus just WHAT failed?

slides.title: Recording API Calls
slides.lead: The denial message disappears once the screen closes, so AWS CloudTrail records management API calls, and data events such as S3 object actions only when a trail logs them

points.text: Logs eventName, errorCode and the calling userIdentity per request
AccessDenied errorCode isolates failed calls from successful ones
Found under CloudTrail Event History in the AWS console
Retained for 90 days by default, longer with a configured trail

slides.notes: Point to errorCode as the field that lets filtering find every denial across thousands of calls. Exam hook: ask what distinguishes a log from the error message shown to the user.

slides.title: From Error To Rule
slides.lead: User alice (arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/alice) calls s3:DeleteObject on finance-reports/q1.csv from IP 203.0.113.5 and receives AccessDenied; the three evidence pieces trace this to one rule

cards: Message shows principal alice, action DeleteObject, resource q1.csv
Shows source IP 203.0.113.5, time of call, and mfaAuthenticated: false
Policy AllowS3ReadWrite permits DeleteObject on the finance-reports bucket
Policy DenyWithoutMFA denies the action when the user has signed in without MFA (condition aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false)
Statement Sid DenyDeleteWithoutMFA is the one overriding the allow

slides.notes: Walk the arrows left to right, ending on the one Sid. Note that an explicit deny beats any allow, which is why MFA absence wins here even though another policy allows the action.

slides.title: From Error To Rule

cells: Confirms the call, its errorCode and source IP (needs a trail that logs S3 data events)
The exact Sid causing the deny

slides.notes: Walk the arrows left to right, ending on the one Sid. Note that an explicit deny beats any allow, which is why MFA absence wins here even though another policy allows the action.

slides.title: Evidence To Action
slides.lead: A traced denial points at one statement, turning a vague failure into a specific, fixable policy line rather than a guess

points.text: Message narrows the search to one principal and action
Audit log confirms the API call was made and records the resulting error
Fix options: add allow, remove deny, or satisfy its condition

slides.notes: Close by stressing that this trace habit is what separates guessing from fixing IAM issues quickly. Common interview question: describe how to debug an AccessDenied error end to end.

Key Takeaways
1. Identity in the Cloud: Root & owner account; users; groups
2. Authentication vs Authorization: Identity verification vs permission checking; credentials: passwords, access keys & tokens
3. Policy Structure: Effect, action, resource & condition; identity-based vs resource-based policies
4. Policy Evaluation Logic: Default deny; explicit allow; explicit deny precedence; combining multiple policies
5. Reading a Denial: Access-denied messages; audit logs; tracing a denial to its statement
